context_blurb:
A scientific claim stands on evidence, not on who backs it. Last century, Stalin's government banned genetics, and American states sterilised thousands of people on the word of eugenics experts; today's rules for experiments on people grew from such harm.

Winter wheat bears grain only after a winter's cold. In the late 1920s the Soviet agronomist Trofim Lysenko wetted and chilled the seed, so wheat sown in spring headed that summer, and he claimed the change would pass to the next generation. Only one result could have shown that: seed from chilled plants, sown in spring without any chill of its own, still bearing grain. Plant biologists have since found that the chilled state is wiped clean in each new embryo, so every generation needs its own winter.

Lysenko also dismissed genes and Mendel's laws, which predict a three-to-one split of forms among a hybrid's offspring. In 1939 Ermolaeva, backed by Lysenko, published counts that she said proved the ratio false. Real counts scatter around any ratio, as a hundred coin tosses rarely land exactly fifty-fifty. In 1940 Andrey Kolmogorov, a mathematician, showed that her counts strayed from Mendel's ratio no more than chance allows, and no less: a new confirmation of Mendel's laws.

Soviet leaders wanted Lysenko's quick promises after the famine of the early 1930s, when breeding by genetics looked slow. With Stalin's approval, Lysenko's side won outright at a farm-science meeting in August 1948. Genetics was barred from teaching and research, and more than 3,000 biologists were dismissed or jailed. A directive soon ordered every stock of Drosophila fruit flies destroyed, among the creatures genetics labs most often bred to study heredity.

Lysenko denied that plants of one kind compete, so crews planting forest belts under a 1948 plan packed acorns into dense clumps, his "nests". By 1951, the ecologist Vladimir Sukachev recorded, not one nest-sown tree in the Ural lands was alive. Critics blamed the crowding, since seedlings of one kind compete hardest for the same light, water and nutrients. A fair test would have set the nests beside oaks sown singly on the same ground in the same years, so that crowding was the only difference.

His rival Nikolai Vavilov built in Leningrad the greatest crop-seed store of its day, full of landraces, the old local kinds, and the wild cousins of crops. He judged modern crops, bred alike, too uniform to resist new diseases, while old and wild kinds hold traits, such as drought resistance, that breeders can cross into new crops. In 1940 the secret police arrested him for opposing Lysenko, and in 1943 he died of starvation in prison.

In America, eugenics, the plan to breed better people by keeping the "unfit" from becoming parents, was taught in the early 1900s as science. Charles Davenport's Eugenics Record Office, founded in 1910, drew up family trees and counted poverty and "feeblemindedness" as inherited because they ran in families. But a family shares its home, food, schooling and poverty as well as its genes, so a family tree can never tell whether genes or a shared upbringing caused a trait. Davenport even sought genes for pellagra, which proved to come from a missing vitamin.

Under Virginia's 1924 sterilisation law, drafted on Harry Laughlin's model, the state colony's head, Albert Priddy, chose a young inmate, Carrie Buck, as the test case. Laughlin swore that her condition was inherited without ever meeting her: the historian Paul Lombardo found that his statement repeated what the colony's doctors had told him.

In 1927 the Supreme Court let Virginia sterilise Carrie, counting her baby Vivian as a third generation on a social worker's remark and one failed infant test. Vivian was placed on the honour roll in first grade, in April 1931; Stephen Jay Gould, who studied her school records, called her a perfectly normal, quite average student.

In 1947 three American judges at Nuremberg, trying Nazi doctors whose experiments had killed many prisoners, wrote ten rules for human experiments into their verdict. The first rule calls the voluntary consent of the person tested absolutely essential: he must choose freely, without force or fraud, and understand what he agrees to. The ninth lets the volunteer end the experiment himself if going on seems impossible to him: his own judgement is enough, with no one's leave, no reasons owed and no proof of harm. The tenth separately bids the scientist in charge halt the work if it is likely to injure, disable or kill.
